summary: Defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base for the ISO connectionless network protocol, ISO 8473, and the End System to Intermediate System protocol, ISO 9542. It is not a standard. It was replaced by RFC 1238.

eli5.summary: A checklist of facts that a device using the ISO kind of network can report about itself.

questions: end system intermediate system protocol management
subtitle: A set of monitoring objects for the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol and End System to Intermediate System protocol.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a way to monitor and collect statistics from devices running the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) and the End System to Intermediate System (ES-IS) protocol, especially as the Internet community experimented with OSI-based networking.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) compatible with SNMP, specifying managed objects that represent CLNP statistics, configuration, and error information that can be queried and monitored.
tldr.outcome: This experimental MIB enabled monitoring of CLNP and ES-IS networks, but was later superseded by RFC 1238, which provided updated and more comprehensive management objects for these protocols.

facts.label: Defined object groups
facts.value: 4 (CLNP, CLNP Error, ES-IS, plus interfaces and routing tables)

facts.label: NSAP address size
facts.value: 1 to 21 octets (first octet is length, max 20 octet NSAP)

today: RFC 1162 is an Experimental protocol from June 1990 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1238. It represented the Internet community's early efforts to manage OSI-based networks alongside TCP/IP, though OSI networking did not achieve widespread adoption.

sections.title: Network Management and MIB Basics
sections.content:
Network management is the process of monitoring and controlling devices on a network. The Management Information Base (MIB) is a virtual information store that allows network administrators to query and manage network devices using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

RFC 1162 defines an experimental portion of the MIB for use with devices running the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) and the End System to Intermediate System (ES-IS) protocol. Unlike most MIB objects which target TCP/IP networks, these objects specifically monitor OSI-based network protocols. This was an important part of the Internet community's work to develop network management standards that could work with both TCP/IP and emerging OSI protocols.
sections.eli5: A Management Information Base is like a report card that a network device fills out about itself. SNMP is how administrators ask for that report card and read the answers.

sections.title: CLNP and ES-IS Protocols
sections.content:
The ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP), defined in ISO 8473, is a network layer protocol similar to IP (Internet Protocol) but designed for OSI networks. It provides connectionless datagram service—each packet is independent and may follow different paths through the network.

The End System to Intermediate System (ES-IS) protocol, defined in ISO 9542, is a neighbor discovery mechanism that operates at the network layer. End Systems (like computers) use ES-IS to discover Intermediate Systems (routers) on their local network segment, and to announce their own availability to neighboring systems. This protocol helps devices maintain reachability information about each other.

These RFC defines management objects that allow administrators to monitor the behavior and statistics of both CLNP datagram forwarding and ES-IS neighbor discovery.
sections.eli5: CLNP is like the postal system for ISO networks, delivering independent packages (datagram). ES-IS is how neighbors in the same neighborhood find each other.

sections.title: Monitored Objects and Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is organized into four logical groups of managed objects. The CLNP Group tracks forwarding decisions and basic statistics: whether a device is acting as an end system or intermediate system (router), the default lifetime value for datagrams, counts of received PDUs, errors detected in headers, invalid destination addresses, forwarded PDUs, dropped PDUs, and discarded PDUs for various reasons.

The CLNP Error Group tracks the CLNP Error protocol, recording counters for error PDUs received and sent, and breaking down incoming errors by type: unspecified errors, protocol procedure errors, checksum failures, congestion-related drops, and header syntax errors.

The ES-IS Group tracks the End System to Intermediate System protocol, with counters for the different types of ES-IS messages: ESH PDUs (End System Hello, sent by end systems), ISH PDUs (Intermediate System Hello, sent by routers), and RDU PDUs (Redirect/Update messages), tracked both for incoming and outgoing directions.

Each managed object has read/write access rules, syntax definitions, and a status indicating whether implementation is mandatory or optional.
sections.eli5: The MIB collects numbers for three kinds of things: how much CLNP traffic flows through, what kinds of errors happen, and how often neighbors say hello to each other.

sections.title: How Administrators Use the MIB
sections.content:
Using SNMP, a network management station can query any object in the CLNP MIB to retrieve statistics or change configuration. For example, an administrator could check clnpInReceives to see the total number of PDUs received, or examine clnpInHdrErrors to detect problems with malformed packets.

The Interfaces and Routing tables allow tracking of per-interface statistics and per-destination routing entries. The Address Translation tables map between CLNP addresses (called NSAPs—Network Service Access Points) and underlying medium addresses, similar to Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) tables in IP networks.

The clnpForwarding object can be set to configure whether a device should forward packets (acting as an intermediate system) or only process packets destined for itself (acting as an end system). Because the MIB is defined using ASN.1 and SMI (Structure of Management Information), it can be easily extended with new objects in future versions.
sections.eli5: An administrator can use SNMP to ask a device how many packets arrived, whether any were broken, and whether it is a router or just a regular computer.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 1162 was published in June 1990 as an Experimental protocol. As stated in the document, it was not a standard, and the expectation was that after experimentation and reaching consensus in the Internet community, the objects might be refined and included in the Internet-standard MIB.

The RFC was intended as an extension mechanism for the base MIB using the experimental object identifier subtree, allowing new objects to be tested before being formally standardized. The design drew on the successful short-term strategy of defining SNMP and the MIB-II for TCP/IP networks.

RFC 1162 is an Experimental status protocol that has been obsoleted by RFC 1238, which provided updated CLNP and ES-IS management information base definitions.
sections.eli5: This was a test version that let people try out new ways to monitor ISO networks before deciding on the final standard. Later, RFC 1238 became the official version.
